19: <!-- overview -->
20: 
21: If you want to control traffic flow at the IP address or port level for TCP, UDP, and SCTP protocols,
22: then you might consider using Kubernetes NetworkPolicies for particular applications in your cluster.
23: NetworkPolicies are an application-centric construct which allow you to specify how a
24: {{< glossary_tooltip text="pod" term_id="pod">}} is allowed to communicate with various network
25: "entities" (we use the word "entity" here to avoid overloading the more common terms such as
26: "endpoints" and "services", which have specific Kubernetes connotations) over the network.
27: NetworkPolicies apply to a connection with a pod on one or both ends, and are not relevant to
28: other connections.
29: 
30: The entities that a Pod can communicate with are identified through a combination of the following
31: three identifiers:
32: 
33: 1. Other pods that are allowed (exception: a pod cannot block access to itself)
34: 1. Namespaces that are allowed
35: 1. IP blocks (exception: traffic to and from the node where a Pod is running is always allowed,
36:    regardless of the IP address of the Pod or the node)
37: 
38: When defining a pod- or namespace-based NetworkPolicy, you use a
39: {{< glossary_tooltip text="selector" term_id="selector">}} to specify what traffic is allowed to
40: and from the Pod(s) that match the selector.
41: 
42: Meanwhile, when IP-based NetworkPolicies are created, we define policies based on IP blocks (CIDR ranges).
43: 
44: <!-- body -->
45: ## Prerequisites
46: 
47: Network policies are implemented by the [network plugin](/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/network-plugins/).
48: To use network policies, you must be using a networking solution which supports NetworkPolicy.
49: Creating a NetworkPolicy resource without a controller that implements it will have no effect.
50: 
51: ## The two sorts of pod isolation
52: 
53: There are two sorts of isolation for a pod: isolation for egress, and isolation for ingress.
54: They concern what connections may be established. "Isolation" here is not absolute, rather it
55: means "some restrictions apply". The alternative, "non-isolated for $direction", means that no
56: restrictions apply in the stated direction. The two sorts of isolation (or not) are declared
57: independently, and are both relevant for a connection from one pod to another.
58: 
59: By default, a pod is non-isolated for egress; all outbound connections are allowed.
60: A pod is isolated for egress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and has
61: "Egress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for egress.
62: When a pod is isolated for egress, the only allowed connections from the pod are those allowed by
63: the `egress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to the pod for egress. Reply traffic for those
64: allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
65: The effects of those `egress` lists combine additively.
66: 
67: By default, a pod is non-isolated for ingress; all inbound connections are allowed.
68: A pod is isolated for ingress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and
69: has "Ingress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for ingress.
70: When a pod is isolated for ingress, the only allowed connections into the pod are those from
71: the pod's node and those allowed by the `ingress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to
72: the pod for ingress. Reply traffic for those allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
73: The effects of those `ingress` lists combine additively.
74: 
75: Network policies do not conflict; they are additive. If any policy or policies apply to a given
76: pod for a given direction, the connections allowed in that direction from that pod is the union of
77: what the applicable policies allow. Thus, order of evaluation does not affect the policy result.
78: 
79: For a connection from a source pod to a destination pod to be allowed, both the egress policy on
80: the source pod and the ingress policy on the destination pod need to allow the connection. If
81: either side does not allow the connection, it will not happen.
82: 
83: ## The NetworkPolicy resource {#networkpolicy-resource}
84: 
85: See the [NetworkPolicy](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#networkpolicy-v1-networking-k8s-io)
86: reference for a full definition of the resource.
87: 
88: An example NetworkPolicy might look like this:
89: 
90: {{% code_sample file="service/networking/networkpolicy.yaml" %}}
91: 
92: {{< note >}}
93: POSTing this to the API server for your cluster will have no effect unless your chosen networking
94: solution supports network policy.
95: {{< /note >}}
96: 
97: __Mandatory Fields__: As with all other Kubernetes config, a NetworkPolicy needs `apiVersion`,
98: `kind`, and `metadata` fields. For general information about working with config files, see
99: [Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-pod-configmap/),
100: and [Object Management](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/object-management).
101: 
102: **spec**: NetworkPolicy [spec](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md#spec-and-status)
103: has all the information needed to define a particular network policy in the given namespace.
104: 
105: **podSelector**: Each NetworkPolicy includes a `podSelector` which selects the grouping of pods to
106: which the policy applies. The example policy selects pods with the label "role=db". An empty
107: `podSelector` selects all pods in the namespace.
108: 
109: **policyTypes**: Each NetworkPolicy includes a `policyTypes` list which may include either
110: `Ingress`, `Egress`, or both. The `policyTypes` field indicates whether or not the given policy
111: applies to ingress traffic to selected pod, egress traffic from selected pods, or both. If no
112: `policyTypes` are specified on a NetworkPolicy then by default `Ingress` will always be set and
113: `Egress` will be set if the NetworkPolicy has any egress rules.
114: 
115: **ingress**: Each NetworkPolicy may include a list of allowed `ingress` rules. Each rule allows
116: traffic which matches both the `from` and `ports` sections. The example policy contains a single
117: rule, which matches traffic on a single port, from one of three sources, the first specified via
118: an `ipBlock`, the second via a `namespaceSelector` and the third via a `podSelector`.
119: 
120: **egress**: Each NetworkPolicy may include a list of allowed `egress` rules. Each rule allows
121: traffic which matches both the `to` and `ports` sections. The example policy contains a single
122: rule, which matches traffic on a single port to any destination in `10.0.0.0/24`.
123: 
124: So, the example NetworkPolicy:
125: 
126: 1. isolates `role=db` pods in the `default` namespace for both ingress and egress traffic
127:    (if they weren't already isolated)
128: 1. (Ingress rules) allows connections to all pods in the `default` namespace with the label
129:    `role=db` on TCP port 6379 from:
130: 
131:    * any pod in the `default` namespace with the label `role=frontend`
132:    * any pod in a namespace with the label `project=myproject`
133:    * IP addresses in the ranges `172.17.0.0`–`172.17.0.255` and `172.17.2.0`–`172.17.255.255`
134:      (ie, all of `172.17.0.0/16` except `172.17.1.0/24`)
135: 
136: 1. (Egress rules) allows connections from any pod in the `default` namespace with the label
137:    `role=db` to CIDR `10.0.0.0/24` on TCP port 5978
138: 
139: See the [Declare Network Policy](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/declare-network-policy/)
140: walkthrough for further examples.
141: 
142: ## Behavior of `to` and `from` selectors
143: 
144: There are four kinds of selectors that can be specified in an `ingress` `from` section or `egress`
145: `to` section:
146: 
147: **podSelector**: This selects particular Pods in the same namespace as the NetworkPolicy which
148: should be allowed as ingress sources or egress destinations.
149: 
150: **namespaceSelector**: This selects particular namespaces for which all Pods should be allowed as
151: ingress sources or egress destinations.
152: 
153: **namespaceSelector** *and* **podSelector**: A single `to`/`from` entry that specifies both
154: `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` selects particular Pods within particular namespaces. Be
155: careful to use correct YAML syntax. For example:
156: 
157: ```yaml
158:   ...
159:   ingress:
160:   - from:
161:     - namespaceSelector:
162:         matchLabels:
163:           user: alice
164:       podSelector:
165:         matchLabels:
166:           role: client
167:   ...
168: ```
169: 
170: This policy contains a single `from` element allowing connections from Pods with the label
171: `role=client` in namespaces with the label `user=alice`. But the following policy is different:
172: 
173: ```yaml
174:   ...
175:   ingress:
176:   - from:
177:     - namespaceSelector:
178:         matchLabels:
179:           user: alice
180:     - podSelector:
181:         matchLabels:
182:           role: client
183:   ...
184: ```
185: 
186: It contains two elements in the `from` array, and allows connections from Pods in the local
187: Namespace with the label `role=client`, *or* from any Pod in any namespace with the label
188: `user=alice`.
189: 
190: When in doubt, use `kubectl describe` to see how Kubernetes has interpreted the policy.
191: 
192: <a name="behavior-of-ipblock-selectors"></a>
193: **ipBlock**: This selects particular IP CIDR ranges to allow as ingress sources or egress
194: destinations. These should be cluster-external IPs, since Pod IPs are ephemeral and unpredictable.
195: 
196: Cluster ingress and egress mechanisms often require rewriting the source or destination IP
197: of packets. In cases where this happens, it is not defined whether this happens before or
198: after NetworkPolicy processing, and the behavior may be different for different
199: combinations of network plugin, cloud provider, `Service` implementation, etc.
200: 
201: In the case of ingress, this means that in some cases you may be able to filter incoming
202: packets based on the actual original source IP, while in other cases, the "source IP" that
203: the NetworkPolicy acts on may be the IP of a `LoadBalancer` or of the Pod's node, etc.
204: 
205: For egress, this means that connections from pods to `Service` IPs that get rewritten to
206: cluster-external IPs may or may not be subject to `ipBlock`-based policies.
207: 
208: ## Default policies
209: 
210: By default, if no policies exist in a namespace, then all ingress and egress traffic is allowed to
211: and from pods in that namespace. The following examples let you change the default behavior
212: in that namespace.
213: 
214: ### Default deny all ingress traffic
215: 
216: You can create a "default" ingress isolation policy for a namespace by creating a NetworkPolicy
217: that selects all pods but does not allow any ingress traffic to those pods.
218:

220: 
221: This ensures that even pods that aren't selected by any other NetworkPolicy will still be isolated
222: for ingress. This policy does not affect isolation for egress from any pod.
223: 
224: ### Allow all ingress traffic

227: that explicitly allows that.

231: With this policy in place, no additional policy or policies can cause any incoming connection to
232: those pods to be denied. This policy has no effect on isolation for egress from any pod.
233: 
234: ### Default deny all egress traffic
235: 
236: You can create a "default" egress isolation policy for a namespace by creating a NetworkPolicy
237: that selects all pods but does not allow any egress traffic from those pods.
238: 
239: {{% code_sample file="service/networking/network-policy-default-deny-egress.yaml" %}}

241: This ensures that even pods that aren't selected by any other NetworkPolicy will not be allowed
242: egress traffic. This policy does not change the ingress isolation behavior of any pod.
243: 
244: ### Allow all egress traffic
245: 
246: If you want to allow all connections from all pods in a namespace, you can create a policy that
247: explicitly allows all outgoing connections from pods in that namespace.
248: 
249: {{% code_sample file="service/networking/network-policy-allow-all-egress.yaml" %}}
250: 
251: With this policy in place, no additional policy or policies can cause any outgoing connection from
252: those pods to be denied. This policy has no effect on isolation for ingress to any pod.
253: 
254: ### Default deny all ingress and all egress traffic
255: 
256: You can create a "default" policy for a namespace which prevents all ingress AND egress traffic by
257: creating the following NetworkPolicy in that namespace.
258:

260: 
261: This ensures that even pods that aren't selected by any other NetworkPolicy will not be allowed
262: ingress or egress traffic.
263: 
264: ## Network traffic filtering
265: 
266: NetworkPolicy is defined for [layer 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OSI_model#Layer_4:_Transport_layer)
267: connections (TCP, UDP, and optionally SCTP). For all the other protocols, the behaviour may vary
268: across network plugins.
269: 
270: {{< note >}}
271: You must be using a {{< glossary_tooltip text="CNI" term_id="cni" >}} plugin that supports SCTP
272: protocol NetworkPolicies.
273: {{< /note >}}
274: 
275: When a `deny all` network policy is defined, it is only guaranteed to deny TCP, UDP and SCTP
276: connections. For other protocols, such as ARP or ICMP, the behaviour is undefined.
277: The same applies to allow rules: when a specific pod is allowed as ingress source or egress destination,
278: it is undefined what happens with (for example) ICMP packets. Protocols such as ICMP may be allowed by some
279: network plugins and denied by others.
280: 
281: ## Targeting a range of ports
282: 
283: {{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.25" state="stable" >}}
284: 
285: When writing a NetworkPolicy, you can target a range of ports instead of a single port.
286: 
287: This is achievable with the usage of the `endPort` field, as the following example:
288: 
289: {{% code_sample file="service/networking/networkpolicy-multiport-egress.yaml" %}}
290: 
291: The above rule allows any Pod with label `role=db` on the namespace `default` to communicate
292: with any IP within the range `10.0.0.0/24` over TCP, provided that the target
293: port is between the range 32000 and 32768.
294: 
295: The following restrictions apply when using this field:
296: 
297: * The `endPort` field must be equal to or greater than the `port` field.
298: * `endPort` can only be defined if `port` is also defined.
299: * Both ports must be numeric.
300: 
301: {{< note >}}
302: Your cluster must be using a {{< glossary_tooltip text="CNI" term_id="cni" >}} plugin that
303: supports the `endPort` field in NetworkPolicy specifications.
304: If your [network plugin](/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/network-plugins/)
305: does not support the `endPort` field and you specify a NetworkPolicy with that,
306: the policy will be applied only for the single `port` field.
307: {{< /note >}}
308: 
309: ## Targeting multiple namespaces by label
310: 
311: In this scenario, your `Egress` NetworkPolicy targets more than one namespace using their
312: label names. For this to work, you need to label the target namespaces. For example:
313: 
314: ```shell
315: kubectl label namespace frontend namespace=frontend
316: kubectl label namespace backend namespace=backend
317: ```
318: 
319: Add the labels under `namespaceSelector` in your NetworkPolicy document. For example:
320: 
321: ```yaml
322: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
323: kind: NetworkPolicy
324: metadata:
325:   name: egress-namespaces
326: spec:
327:   podSelector:
328:     matchLabels:
329:       app: myapp
330:   policyTypes:
331:   - Egress
332:   egress:
333:   - to:
334:     - namespaceSelector:
335:         matchExpressions:
336:         - key: namespace
337:           operator: In
338:           values: ["frontend", "backend"]
339: ```
340: 
341: {{< note >}}
342: It is not possible to directly specify the name of the namespaces in a NetworkPolicy.
343: You must use a `namespaceSelector` with `matchLabels` or `matchExpressions` to select the
344: namespaces based on their labels.
345: {{< /note >}}
346: 
347: ## Targeting a Namespace by its name
348: 
349: The Kubernetes control plane sets an immutable label `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` on all
350: namespaces, the value of the label is the namespace name.
351: 
352: While NetworkPolicy cannot target a namespace by its name with some object field, you can use the
353: standardized label to target a specific namespace.
354: 
355: ## Pod lifecycle
356: 
357: {{< note >}}
358: The following applies to clusters with a conformant networking plugin and a conformant implementation of
359: NetworkPolicy.
360: {{< /note >}}
361: 
362: When a new NetworkPolicy object is created, it may take some time for a network plugin
363: to handle the new object. If a pod that is affected by a NetworkPolicy
364: is created before the network plugin has completed NetworkPolicy handling,
365: that pod may be started unprotected, and isolation rules will be applied when
366: the NetworkPolicy handling is completed.
367: 
368: Once the NetworkPolicy is handled by a network plugin,
369: 
370: 1. All newly created pods affected by a given NetworkPolicy will be isolated before they are started.
371:    Implementations of NetworkPolicy must ensure that filtering is effective throughout
372:    the Pod lifecycle, even from the very first instant that any container in that Pod is started.
373:    Because they are applied at Pod level, NetworkPolicies apply equally to init containers,
374:    sidecar containers, and regular containers.
375: 
376: 1. Allow rules will be applied eventually after the isolation rules (or may be applied at the same time).
377:    In the worst case, a newly created pod may have no network connectivity at all when it is first started, if
378:    isolation rules were already applied, but no allow rules were applied yet.
379: 
380: Every created NetworkPolicy will be handled by a network plugin eventually, but there is no
381: way to tell from the Kubernetes API when exactly that happens.
382: 
383: Therefore, pods must be resilient against being started up with different network
384: connectivity than expected. If you need to make sure the pod can reach certain destinations
385: before being started, you can use an [init container](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/init-containers/)
386: to wait for those destinations to be reachable before kubelet starts the app containers.
387: 
388: Every NetworkPolicy will be applied to all selected pods eventually.
389: Because the network plugin may implement NetworkPolicy in a distributed manner,
390: it is possible that pods may see a slightly inconsistent view of network policies
391: when the pod is first created, or when pods or policies change.
392: For example, a newly-created pod that is supposed to be able to reach both Pod A
393: on Node 1 and Pod B on Node 2 may find that it can reach Pod A immediately,
394: but cannot reach Pod B until a few seconds later.
395: 
396: ## NetworkPolicy and `hostNetwork` pods
397: 
398: NetworkPolicy behaviour for `hostNetwork` pods is undefined, but it should be limited to 2 possibilities:
399: 
400: - The network plugin can distinguish `hostNetwork` pod traffic from all other traffic
401:   (including being able to distinguish traffic from different `hostNetwork` pods on
402:   the same node), and will apply NetworkPolicy to `hostNetwork` pods just like it does
403:   to pod-network pods.
404: - The network plugin cannot properly distinguish `hostNetwork` pod traffic,
405:   and so it ignores `hostNetwork` pods when matching `podSelector` and `namespaceSelector`.
406:   Traffic to/from `hostNetwork` pods is treated the same as all other traffic to/from the node IP.
407:   (This is the most common implementation.)
408: 
409: This applies when
410: 
411: 1. a `hostNetwork` pod is selected by `spec.podSelector`.
412:    
413:    ```yaml
414:      ...
415:      spec:
416:        podSelector:
417:          matchLabels:
418:            role: client
419:      ...
420:    ```
421:  
422: 1. a `hostNetwork` pod is selected by a `podSelector` or `namespaceSelector` in an `ingress` or `egress` rule.
423: 
424:    ```yaml
425:      ...
426:      ingress:
427:        - from:
428:          - podSelector:
429:              matchLabels:
430:                role: client
431:      ...
432:    ```
433: 
434: At the same time, since `hostNetwork` pods have the same IP addresses as the nodes they reside on,
435: their connections will be treated as node connections. For example, you can allow traffic
436: from a `hostNetwork` Pod using an `ipBlock` rule.
437: 
438: ## What you can't do with network policies (at least, not yet)
439: 
440: As of Kubernetes {{< skew currentVersion >}}, the following functionality does not exist in the
441: NetworkPolicy API, but you might be able to implement workarounds using Operating System
442: components (such as SELinux, OpenVSwitch, IPTables, and so on) or Layer 7 technologies (Ingress
443: controllers, Service Mesh implementations) or admission controllers. In case you are new to
444: network security in Kubernetes, its worth noting that the following User Stories cannot (yet) be
445: implemented using the NetworkPolicy API.
446: 
447: - Forcing internal cluster traffic to go through a common gateway (this might be best served with
448:   a service mesh or other proxy).
449: - Anything TLS related (use a service mesh or ingress controller for this).
450: - Node specific policies (you can use CIDR notation for these, but you cannot target nodes by
451:   their Kubernetes identities specifically).
452: - Targeting of services by name (you can, however, target pods or namespaces by their
453:   {{< glossary_tooltip text="labels" term_id="label" >}}, which is often a viable workaround).
454: - Creation or management of "Policy requests" that are fulfilled by a third party.
455: - Default policies which are applied to all namespaces or pods (there are some third party
456:   Kubernetes distributions and projects which can do this).
457: - Advanced policy querying and reachability tooling.
458: - The ability to log network security events (for example connections that are blocked or accepted).
459: - The ability to explicitly deny policies (currently the model for NetworkPolicies are deny by
460:   default, with only the ability to add allow rules).
461: - The ability to prevent loopback or incoming host traffic (Pods cannot currently block localhost
462:   access, nor do they have the ability to block access from their resident node).
463: 
464: ## NetworkPolicy's impact on existing connections
465: 
466: When the set of NetworkPolicies that applies to an existing connection changes - this could happen
467: either due to a change in NetworkPolicies or if the relevant labels of the namespaces/pods selected by the
468: policy (both subject and peers) are changed in the middle of an existing connection - it is
469: implementation defined as to whether the change will take effect for that existing connection or not.
470: Example: A policy is created that leads to denying a previously allowed connection, the underlying network plugin
471: implementation is responsible for defining if that new policy will close the existing connections or not.
472: It is recommended not to modify policies/pods/namespaces in ways that might affect existing connections.
473:

477:   walkthrough for further examples.
478: - See more [recipes](https://github.com/ahmetb/kubernetes-network-policy-recipes) for common
479:   scenarios enabled by the NetworkPolicy resource.

18: 
19: A Secret is an object that contains a small amount of sensitive data such as
20: a password, a token, or a key. Such information might otherwise be put in a
21: {{< glossary_tooltip term_id="pod" >}} specification or in a
22: {{< glossary_tooltip text="container image" term_id="image" >}}. Using a
23: Secret means that you don't need to include confidential data in your
24: application code.
25: 
26: Because Secrets can be created independently of the Pods that use them, there
27: is less risk of the Secret (and its data) being exposed during the workflow of
28: creating, viewing, and editing Pods. Kubernetes, and applications that run in
29: your cluster, can also take additional precautions with Secrets, such as avoiding
30: writing sensitive data to nonvolatile storage.
31: 
32: Secrets are similar to {{< glossary_tooltip text="ConfigMaps" term_id="configmap" >}}
33: but are specifically intended to hold confidential data.
34: 
35: {{< caution >}}
36: Kubernetes Secrets are, by default, stored unencrypted in the API server's underlying data store
37: (etcd). Anyone with API access can retrieve or modify a Secret, and so can anyone with access to etcd.
38: Additionally, anyone who is authorized to create a Pod in a namespace can use that access to read
39: any Secret in that namespace; this includes indirect access such as the ability to create a
40: Deployment.
41: 
42: In order to safely use Secrets, take at least the following steps:
43: 
44: 1. [Enable Encryption at Rest](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/encrypt-data/) for Secrets.
45: 1. [Enable or configure RBAC rules](/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authorization/) with
46:    least-privilege access to Secrets.
47: 1. Restrict Secret access to specific containers.
48: 1. [Consider using external Secret store providers](https://secrets-store-csi-driver.sigs.k8s.io/concepts.html#provider-for-the-secrets-store-csi-driver).
49: 
50: For more guidelines to manage and improve the security of your Secrets, refer to
51: [Good practices for Kubernetes Secrets](/docs/concepts/security/secrets-good-practices).
52: 
53: {{< /caution >}}
54: 
55: See [Information security for Secrets](#information-security-for-secrets) for more details.
56:

58: 
59: ## Uses for Secrets
60: 
61: You can use Secrets for purposes such as the following:
62: 
63: - [Set environment variables for a container](/docs/tasks/inject-data-application/distribute-credentials-secure/#define-container-environment-variables-using-secret-data).
64: - [Provide credentials such as SSH keys or passwords to Pods](/docs/tasks/inject-data-application/distribute-credentials-secure/#provide-prod-test-creds).
65: - [Allow the kubelet to pull container images from private registries](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/pull-image-private-registry/).
66: 
67: The Kubernetes control plane also uses Secrets; for example,
68: [bootstrap token Secrets](#bootstrap-token-secrets) are a mechanism to
69: help automate node registration.
70: 
71: ### Use case: dotfiles in a secret volume
72: 
73: You can make your data "hidden" by defining a key that begins with a dot.
74: This key represents a dotfile or "hidden" file. For example, when the following Secret
75: is mounted into a volume, `secret-volume`, the volume will contain a single file,
76: called `.secret-file`, and the `dotfile-test-container` will have this file
77: present at the path `/etc/secret-volume/.secret-file`.
78: 
79: {{< note >}}
80: Files beginning with dot characters are hidden from the output of `ls -l`;
81: you must use `ls -la` to see them when listing directory contents.
82: {{< /note >}}
83: 
84: {{% code language="yaml" file="secret/dotfile-secret.yaml" %}}
85: 
86: ### Use case: Secret visible to one container in a Pod
87: 
88: Consider a program that needs to handle HTTP requests, do some complex business
89: logic, and then sign some messages with an HMAC. Because it has complex
90: application logic, there might be an unnoticed remote file reading exploit in
91: the server, which could expose the private key to an attacker.
92: 
93: This could be divided into two processes in two containers: a frontend container
94: which handles user interaction and business logic, but which cannot see the
95: private key; and a signer container that can see the private key, and responds
96: to simple signing requests from the frontend (for example, over localhost networking).
97: 
98: With this partitioned approach, an attacker now has to trick the application
99: server into doing something rather arbitrary, which may be harder than getting
100: it to read a file.
101: 
102: ### Alternatives to Secrets
103: 
104: Rather than using a Secret to protect confidential data, you can pick from alternatives.
105: 
106: Here are some of your options:
107: 
108: - If your cloud-native component needs to authenticate to another application that you
109:   know is running within the same Kubernetes cluster, you can use a
110:   [ServiceAccount](/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication/#service-account-tokens)
111:   and its tokens to identify your client.
112: - There are third-party tools that you can run, either within or outside your cluster,
113:   that manage sensitive data. For example, a service that Pods access over HTTPS,
114:   that reveals a Secret if the client correctly authenticates (for example, with a ServiceAccount
115:   token).
116: - For authentication, you can implement a custom signer for X.509 certificates, and use
117:   [CertificateSigningRequests](/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/certificate-signing-requests/)
118:   to let that custom signer issue certificates to Pods that need them.
119: - You can use a [device plugin](/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/device-plugins/)
120:   to expose node-local encryption hardware to a specific Pod. For example, you can schedule
121:   trusted Pods onto nodes that provide a Trusted Platform Module, configured out-of-band.
122: 
123: You can also combine two or more of those options, including the option to use Secret objects themselves.
124: 
125: For example: implement (or deploy) an {{< glossary_tooltip text="operator" term_id="operator-pattern" >}}
126: that fetches short-lived session tokens from an external service, and then creates Secrets based
127: on those short-lived session tokens. Pods running in your cluster can make use of the session tokens,
128: and operator ensures they are valid. This separation means that you can run Pods that are unaware of
129: the exact mechanisms for issuing and refreshing those session tokens.
130: 
131: ## Types of Secret {#secret-types}
132: 
133: When creating a Secret, you can specify its type using the `type` field of
134: the [Secret](/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/config-and-storage-resources/secret-v1/)
135: resource, or certain equivalent `kubectl` command line flags (if available).
136: The Secret type is used to facilitate programmatic handling of the Secret data.
137: 
138: Kubernetes provides several built-in types for some common usage scenarios.
139: These types vary in terms of the validations performed and the constraints
140: Kubernetes imposes on them.
141: 
142: | Built-in Type                         | Usage                                   |
143: | ------------------------------------- |---------------------------------------- |
144: | `Opaque`                              | arbitrary user-defined data            |
145: | `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` | ServiceAccount token                    |
146: | `kubernetes.io/dockercfg`             | serialized `~/.dockercfg` file          |
147: | `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`      | serialized `~/.docker/config.json` file |
148: | `kubernetes.io/basic-auth`            | credentials for basic authentication    |
149: | `kubernetes.io/ssh-auth`              | credentials for SSH authentication      |
150: | `kubernetes.io/tls`                   | data for a TLS client or server         |
151: | `bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token`       | bootstrap token data                    |
152: 
153: You can define and use your own Secret type by assigning a non-empty string as the
154: `type` value for a Secret object (an empty string is treated as an `Opaque` type).
155: 
156: Kubernetes doesn't impose any constraints on the type name. However, if you
157: are using one of the built-in types, you must meet all the requirements defined
158: for that type.
159: 
160: If you are defining a type of Secret that's for public use, follow the convention
161: and structure the Secret type to have your domain name before the name, separated
162: by a `/`. For example: `cloud-hosting.example.net/cloud-api-credentials`.
163: 
164: ### Opaque Secrets
165: 
166: `Opaque` is the default Secret type if you don't explicitly specify a type in
167: a Secret manifest. When you create a Secret using `kubectl`, you must use the
168: `generic` subcommand to indicate an `Opaque` Secret type. For example, the
169: following command creates an empty Secret of type `Opaque`:
170: 
171: ```shell
172: kubectl create secret generic empty-secret
173: kubectl get secret empty-secret
174: ```
175: 
176: The output looks like:
177: 
178: ```
179: NAME           TYPE     DATA   AGE
180: empty-secret   Opaque   0      2m6s
181: ```
182: 
183: The `DATA` column shows the number of data items stored in the Secret.
184: In this case, `0` means you have created an empty Secret.
185: 
186: ### ServiceAccount token Secrets
187: 
188: A `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` type of Secret is used to store a
189: token credential that identifies a
190: {{< glossary_tooltip text="ServiceAccount" term_id="service-account" >}}. This
191: is a legacy mechanism that provides long-lived ServiceAccount credentials to
192: Pods.
193: 
194: In Kubernetes v1.22 and later, the recommended approach is to obtain a
195: short-lived, automatically rotating ServiceAccount token by using the
196: [`TokenRequest`](/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/authentication-resources/token-request-v1/)
197: API instead. You can get these short-lived tokens using the following methods:
198: 
199: * Call the `TokenRequest` API either directly or by using an API client like
200:   `kubectl`. For example, you can use the
201:   [`kubectl create token`](/docs/reference/generated/kubectl/kubectl-commands#-em-token-em-)
202:   command.
203: * Request a mounted token in a
204:   [projected volume](/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/service-accounts-admin/#bound-service-account-token-volume)
205:   in your Pod manifest. Kubernetes creates the token and mounts it in the Pod.
206:   The token is automatically invalidated when the Pod that it's mounted in is
207:   deleted. For details, see
208:   [Launch a Pod using service account token projection](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-account/#launch-a-pod-using-service-account-token-projection).
209: 
210: {{< note >}}
211: You should only create a ServiceAccount token Secret
212: if you can't use the `TokenRequest` API to obtain a token,
213: and the security exposure of persisting a non-expiring token credential
214: in a readable API object is acceptable to you. For instructions, see
215: [Manually create a long-lived API token for a ServiceAccount](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-account/#manually-create-an-api-token-for-a-serviceaccount).
216: {{< /note >}}
217: 
218: When using this Secret type, you need to ensure that the
219: `kubernetes.io/service-account.name` annotation is set to an existing
220: ServiceAccount name. If you are creating both the ServiceAccount and
221: the Secret objects, you should create the ServiceAccount object first.
222: 
223: After the Secret is created, a Kubernetes {{< glossary_tooltip text="controller" term_id="controller" >}}
224: fills in some other fields such as the `kubernetes.io/service-account.uid` annotation, and the
225: `token` key in the `data` field, which is populated with an authentication token.
226: 
227: The following example configuration declares a ServiceAccount token Secret:
228: 
229: {{% code language="yaml" file="secret/serviceaccount-token-secret.yaml" %}}
230: 
231: After creating the Secret, wait for Kubernetes to populate the `token` key in the `data` field.
232: 
233: See the [ServiceAccount](/docs/concepts/security/service-accounts/)
234: documentation for more information on how ServiceAccounts work.
235: You can also check the `automountServiceAccountToken` field and the
236: `serviceAccountName` field of the
237: [`Pod`](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#pod-v1-core)
238: for information on referencing ServiceAccount credentials from within Pods.

240: ### Docker config Secrets
241: 
242: If you are creating a Secret to store credentials for accessing a container image registry,
243: you must use one of the following `type` values for that Secret:
244: 
245: - `kubernetes.io/dockercfg`: store a serialized `~/.dockercfg` which is the
246:   legacy format for configuring Docker command line. The Secret
247:   `data` field contains a `.dockercfg` key whose value is the content of a
248:   base64 encoded `~/.dockercfg` file.
249: - `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`: store a serialized JSON that follows the
250:   same format rules as the `~/.docker/config.json` file, which is a new format
251:   for `~/.dockercfg`. The Secret `data` field must contain a
252:   `.dockerconfigjson` key for which the value is the content of a base64
253:   encoded `~/.docker/config.json` file.
254: 
255: Below is an example for a `kubernetes.io/dockercfg` type of Secret:
256: 
257: {{% code language="yaml" file="secret/dockercfg-secret.yaml" %}}
258: 
259: {{< note >}}
260: If you do not want to perform the base64 encoding, you can choose to use the
261: `stringData` field instead.
262: {{< /note >}}
263: 
264: When you create Docker config Secrets using a manifest, the API
265: server checks whether the expected key exists in the `data` field, and
266: it verifies if the value provided can be parsed as a valid JSON. The API
267: server doesn't validate if the JSON actually is a Docker config file.
268: 
269: You can also use `kubectl` to create a Secret for accessing a container
270: registry, such as when you don't have a Docker configuration file:
271: 
272: ```shell
273: kubectl create secret docker-registry secret-tiger-docker \
274:   --docker-email=tiger@acme.example \
275:   --docker-username=tiger \
276:   --docker-password=pass1234 \
277:   --docker-server=my-registry.example:5000
278: ```
279: 
280: This command creates a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`.
281: 
282: Retrieve the `.data.dockerconfigjson` field from that new Secret and decode the
283: data:
284: 
285: ```shell
286: kubectl get secret secret-tiger-docker -o jsonpath='{.data.*}' | base64 -d
287: ```
288: 
289: The output is equivalent to the following JSON document (which is also a valid
290: Docker configuration file):
291: 
292: ```json
293: {
294:   "auths": {
295:     "my-registry.example:5000": {
296:       "username": "tiger",
297:       "password": "pass1234",
298:       "email": "tiger@acme.example",
299:       "auth": "dGlnZXI6cGFzczEyMzQ="
300:     }
301:   }
302: }
303: ```
304: 
305: {{< caution >}}
306: The `auth` value there is base64 encoded; it is obscured but not secret.
307: Anyone who can read that Secret can learn the registry access bearer token.
308: 
309: It is suggested to use [credential providers](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-credential-provider/) to dynamically and securely provide pull secrets on-demand.
310: {{< /caution >}}

312: ### Basic authentication Secret
313: 
314: The `kubernetes.io/basic-auth` type is provided for storing credentials needed
315: for basic authentication. When using this Secret type, the `data` field of the
316: Secret must contain one of the following two keys:
317: 
318: - `username`: the user name for authentication
319: - `password`: the password or token for authentication
320: 
321: Both values for the above two keys are base64 encoded strings. You can
322: alternatively provide the clear text content using the `stringData` field in the
323: Secret manifest.
324: 
325: The following manifest is an example of a basic authentication Secret:
326:

328: 
329: {{< note >}}
330: The `stringData` field for a Secret does not work well with server-side apply.
331: {{< /note >}}
332: 
333: The basic authentication Secret type is provided only for convenience.
334: You can create an `Opaque` type for credentials used for basic authentication.
335: However, using the defined and public Secret type (`kubernetes.io/basic-auth`) helps other
336: people to understand the purpose of your Secret, and sets a convention for what key names
337: to expect.
338: 
339: ### SSH authentication Secrets
340: 
341: The builtin type `kubernetes.io/ssh-auth` is provided for storing data used in
342: SSH authentication. When using this Secret type, you will have to specify a
343: `ssh-privatekey` key-value pair in the `data` (or `stringData`) field
344: as the SSH credential to use.
345: 
346: The following manifest is an example of a Secret used for SSH public/private
347: key authentication:
348: 
349: {{% code language="yaml" file="secret/ssh-auth-secret.yaml" %}}
350: 
351: The SSH authentication Secret type is provided only for convenience.
352: You can create an `Opaque` type for credentials used for SSH authentication.
353: However, using the defined and public Secret type (`kubernetes.io/ssh-auth`) helps other
354: people to understand the purpose of your Secret, and sets a convention for what key names
355: to expect.
356: The Kubernetes API verifies that the required keys are set for a Secret of this type.
357: 
358: {{< caution >}}
359: SSH private keys do not establish trusted communication between an SSH client and
360: host server on their own. A secondary means of establishing trust is needed to
361: mitigate "man in the middle" attacks, such as a `known_hosts` file added to a ConfigMap.
362: {{< /caution >}}

364: ### TLS Secrets
365: 
366: The `kubernetes.io/tls` Secret type is for storing
367: a certificate and its associated key that are typically used for TLS.
368: 
369: One common use for TLS Secrets is to configure encryption in transit for
370: an [Ingress](/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/), but you can also use it
371: with other resources or directly in your workload.
372: When using this type of Secret, the `tls.key` and the `tls.crt` key must be provided
373: in the `data` (or `stringData`) field of the Secret configuration, although the API
374: server doesn't actually validate the values for each key.
375: 
376: As an alternative to using `stringData`, you can use the `data` field to provide
377: the base64 encoded certificate and private key. For details, see
378: [Constraints on Secret names and data](#restriction-names-data).
379: 
380: The following YAML contains an example config for a TLS Secret:
381: 
382: {{% code language="yaml" file="secret/tls-auth-secret.yaml" %}}
383: 
384: The TLS Secret type is provided only for convenience.
385: You can create an `Opaque` type for credentials used for TLS authentication.
386: However, using the defined and public Secret type (`kubernetes.io/tls`)
387: helps ensure the consistency of Secret format in your project. The API server
388: verifies if the required keys are set for a Secret of this type.
389: 
390: To create a TLS Secret using `kubectl`, use the `tls` subcommand:
391: 
392: ```shell
393: kubectl create secret tls my-tls-secret \
394:   --cert=path/to/cert/file \
395:   --key=path/to/key/file
396: ```
397: 
398: The public/private key pair must exist before hand. The public key certificate for `--cert` must be .PEM encoded
399: and must match the given private key for `--key`.

401: ### Bootstrap token Secrets
402: 
403: The `bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token` Secret type is for
404: tokens used during the node bootstrap process. It stores tokens used to sign
405: well-known ConfigMaps.
406: 
407: A bootstrap token Secret is usually created in the `kube-system` namespace and
408: named in the form `bootstrap-token-<token-id>` where `<token-id>` is a 6 character
409: string of the token ID.
410: 
411: As a Kubernetes manifest, a bootstrap token Secret might look like the
412: following:
413: 
414: {{% code language="yaml" file="secret/bootstrap-token-secret-base64.yaml" %}}
415: 
416: A bootstrap token Secret has the following keys specified under `data`:
417: 
418: - `token-id`: A random 6 character string as the token identifier. Required.
419: - `token-secret`: A random 16 character string as the actual token Secret. Required.
420: - `description`: A human-readable string that describes what the token is
421:   used for. Optional.
422: - `expiration`: An absolute UTC time using [RFC3339](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3339) specifying when the token
423:   should be expired. Optional.
424: - `usage-bootstrap-<usage>`: A boolean flag indicating additional usage for
425:   the bootstrap token.
426: - `auth-extra-groups`: A comma-separated list of group names that will be
427:   authenticated as in addition to the `system:bootstrappers` group.
428: 
429: You can alternatively provide the values in the `stringData` field of the Secret
430: without base64 encoding them:
431: 
432: {{% code language="yaml" file="secret/bootstrap-token-secret-literal.yaml" %}}
433: 
434: {{< note >}}
435: The `stringData` field for a Secret does not work well with server-side apply.
436: {{< /note >}}

438: ## Working with Secrets
439: 
440: ### Creating a Secret
441: 
442: There are several options to create a Secret:
443: 
444: - [Use `kubectl`](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-kubectl/)
445: - [Use a configuration file](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-config-file/)
446: - [Use the Kustomize tool](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-kustomize/)
447: 
448: #### Constraints on Secret names and data {#restriction-names-data}
449: 
450: The name of a Secret object must be a valid
451: [DNS subdomain name](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/names#dns-subdomain-names).
452: 
453: You can specify the `data` and/or the `stringData` field when creating a
454: configuration file for a Secret. The `data` and the `stringData` fields are optional.
455: The values for all keys in the `data` field have to be base64-encoded strings.
456: If the conversion to base64 string is not desirable, you can choose to specify
457: the `stringData` field instead, which accepts arbitrary strings as values.
458: 
459: The keys of `data` and `stringData` must consist of alphanumeric characters,
460: `-`, `_` or `.`. All key-value pairs in the `stringData` field are internally
461: merged into the `data` field. If a key appears in both the `data` and the
462: `stringData` field, the value specified in the `stringData` field takes
463: precedence.
464: 
465: #### Size limit {#restriction-data-size}
466: 
467: Individual Secrets are limited to 1MiB in size. This is to discourage creation
468: of very large Secrets that could exhaust the API server and kubelet memory.
469: However, creation of many smaller Secrets could also exhaust memory. You can
470: use a [resource quota](/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/) to limit the
471: number of Secrets (or other resources) in a namespace.
472: 
473: ### Editing a Secret
474: 
475: You can edit an existing Secret unless it is [immutable](#secret-immutable). To
476: edit a Secret, use one of the following methods:
477: 
478: - [Use `kubectl`](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-kubectl/#edit-secret)
479: - [Use a configuration file](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-config-file/#edit-secret)
480: 
481: You can also edit the data in a Secret using the [Kustomize tool](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-kustomize/#edit-secret). However, this
482: method creates a new `Secret` object with the edited data.
483: 
484: Depending on how you created the Secret, as well as how the Secret is used in
485: your Pods, updates to existing `Secret` objects are propagated automatically to
486: Pods that use the data. For more information, refer to [Using Secrets as files from a Pod](#using-secrets-as-files-from-a-pod) section.
487: 
488: ### Using a Secret
489: 
490: Secrets can be mounted as data volumes or exposed as
491: {{< glossary_tooltip text="environment variables" term_id="container-env-variables" >}}
492: to be used by a container in a Pod. Secrets can also be used by other parts of the
493: system, without being directly exposed to the Pod. For example, Secrets can hold
494: credentials that other parts of the system should use to interact with external
495: systems on your behalf.
496: 
497: Secret volume sources are validated to ensure that the specified object
498: reference actually points to an object of type Secret. Therefore, a Secret
499: needs to be created before any Pods that depend on it.
500: 
501: If the Secret cannot be fetched (perhaps because it does not exist, or
502: due to a temporary lack of connection to the API server) the kubelet
503: periodically retries running that Pod. The kubelet also reports an Event
504: for that Pod, including details of the problem fetching the Secret.
505: 
506: #### Optional Secrets {#restriction-secret-must-exist}
507: 
508: When you reference a Secret in a Pod, you can mark the Secret as _optional_,
509: such as in the following example. If an optional Secret doesn't exist,
510: Kubernetes ignores it.
511: 
512: {{% code language="yaml" file="secret/optional-secret.yaml" %}}
513: 
514: By default, Secrets are required. None of a Pod's containers will start until
515: all non-optional Secrets are available.
516: 
517: If a Pod references a specific key in a non-optional Secret and that Secret
518: does exist, but is missing the named key, the Pod fails during startup.
519: 
520: ### Using Secrets as files from a Pod {#using-secrets-as-files-from-a-pod}
521: 
522: If you want to access data from a Secret in a Pod, one way to do that is to
523: have Kubernetes make the value of that Secret be available as a file inside
524: the filesystem of one or more of the Pod's containers.
525: 
526: For instructions, refer to
527: [Create a Pod that has access to the secret data through a Volume](/docs/tasks/inject-data-application/distribute-credentials-secure/#create-a-pod-that-has-access-to-the-secret-data-through-a-volume).
528: 
529: When a volume contains data from a Secret, and that Secret is updated, Kubernetes tracks
530: this and updates the data in the volume, using an eventually-consistent approach.
531: 
532: {{< note >}}
533: A container using a Secret as a
534: [subPath](/docs/concepts/storage/volumes#using-subpath) volume mount does not receive
535: automated Secret updates.
536: {{< /note >}}
537: 
538: The kubelet keeps a cache of the current keys and values for the Secrets that are used in
539: volumes for pods on that node.
540: You can configure the way that the kubelet detects changes from the cached values. The
541: `configMapAndSecretChangeDetectionStrategy` field in the
542: [kubelet configuration](/docs/reference/config-api/kubelet-config.v1beta1/) controls
543: which strategy the kubelet uses. The default strategy is `Watch`.
544: 
545: Updates to Secrets can be either propagated by an API watch mechanism (the default), based on
546: a cache with a defined time-to-live, or polled from the cluster API server on each kubelet
547: synchronisation loop.
548: 
549: As a result, the total delay from the moment when the Secret is updated to the moment
550: when new keys are projected to the Pod can be as long as the kubelet sync period + cache
551: propagation delay, where the cache propagation delay depends on the chosen cache type
552: (following the same order listed in the previous paragraph, these are:
553: watch propagation delay, the configured cache TTL, or zero for direct polling).
554: 
555: ### Using Secrets as environment variables
556: 
557: To use a Secret in an {{< glossary_tooltip text="environment variable" term_id="container-env-variables" >}}
558: in a Pod:
559: 
560: 1. For each container in your Pod specification, add an environment variable
561:    for each Secret key that you want to use to the
562:    `env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef` field.
563: 1. Modify your image and/or command line so that the program looks for values
564:    in the specified environment variables.
565: 
566: For instructions, refer to
567: [Define container environment variables using Secret data](/docs/tasks/inject-data-application/distribute-credentials-secure/#define-container-environment-variables-using-secret-data).
568: 
569: It's important to note that the range of characters allowed for environment variable
570: names in pods is [restricted](/docs/tasks/inject-data-application/define-environment-variable-container/#using-environment-variables-inside-of-your-config).
571: If any keys do not meet the rules, those keys are not made available to your container, though
572: the Pod is allowed to start.
573: 
574: ### Container image pull Secrets {#using-imagepullsecrets}
575: 
576: If you want to fetch container images from a private repository, you need a way for
577: the kubelet on each node to authenticate to that repository. You can configure
578: _image pull Secrets_ to make this possible. These Secrets are configured at the Pod
579: level.
580: 
581: #### Using imagePullSecrets
582: 
583: The `imagePullSecrets` field is a list of references to Secrets in the same namespace.
584: You can use an `imagePullSecrets` to pass a Secret that contains a Docker (or other) image registry
585: password to the kubelet. The kubelet uses this information to pull a private image on behalf of your Pod.
586: See the [PodSpec API](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#podspec-v1-core)
587: for more information about the `imagePullSecrets` field.
588: 
589: ##### Manually specifying an imagePullSecret
590: 
591: You can learn how to specify `imagePullSecrets` from the
592: [container images](/docs/concepts/containers/images/#specifying-imagepullsecrets-on-a-pod)
593: documentation.
594: 
595: ##### Arranging for imagePullSecrets to be automatically attached
596: 
597: You can manually create `imagePullSecrets`, and reference these from a ServiceAccount. Any Pods
598: created with that ServiceAccount or created with that ServiceAccount by default, will get their
599: `imagePullSecrets` field set to that of the service account.
600: See [Add ImagePullSecrets to a service account](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-account/#add-imagepullsecrets-to-a-service-account)
601: for a detailed explanation of that process.
602: 
603: ### Using Secrets with static Pods {#restriction-static-pod}
604: 
605: You cannot use ConfigMaps or Secrets with {{< glossary_tooltip text="static Pods" term_id="static-pod" >}}.
606: 
607: ## Immutable Secrets {#secret-immutable}
608: 
609: {{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.21" state="stable" >}}
610: 
611: Kubernetes lets you mark specific Secrets (and ConfigMaps) as _immutable_.
612: Preventing changes to the data of an existing Secret has the following benefits:
613: 
614: - protects you from accidental (or unwanted) updates that could cause applications outages
615: - (for clusters that extensively use Secrets - at least tens of thousands of unique Secret
616:   to Pod mounts), switching to immutable Secrets improves the performance of your cluster
617:   by significantly reducing load on kube-apiserver. The kubelet does not need to maintain
618:   a [watch] on any Secrets that are marked as immutable.
619: 
620: ### Marking a Secret as immutable {#secret-immutable-create}
621: 
622: You can create an immutable Secret by setting the `immutable` field to `true`. For example,
623: 
624: ```yaml
625: apiVersion: v1
626: kind: Secret
627: metadata: ...
628: data: ...
629: immutable: true
630: ```
631: 
632: You can also update any existing mutable Secret to make it immutable.
633: 
634: {{< note >}}
635: Once a Secret or ConfigMap is marked as immutable, it is _not_ possible to revert this change
636: nor to mutate the contents of the `data` field. You can only delete and recreate the Secret.
637: Existing Pods maintain a mount point to the deleted Secret - it is recommended to recreate
638: these pods.
639: {{< /note >}}
640: 
641: ## Information security for Secrets
642: 
643: Although ConfigMap and Secret work similarly, Kubernetes applies some additional
644: protection for Secret objects.
645: 
646: Secrets often hold values that span a spectrum of importance, many of which can
647: cause escalations within Kubernetes (e.g. service account tokens) and to
648: external systems. Even if an individual app can reason about the power of the
649: Secrets it expects to interact with, other apps within the same namespace can
650: render those assumptions invalid.
651: 
652: A Secret is only sent to a node if a Pod on that node requires it.
653: For mounting Secrets into Pods, the kubelet stores a copy of the data into a `tmpfs`
654: so that the confidential data is not written to durable storage.
655: Once the Pod that depends on the Secret is deleted, the kubelet deletes its local copy
656: of the confidential data from the Secret.
657: 
658: There may be several containers in a Pod. By default, containers you define
659: only have access to the default ServiceAccount and its related Secret.
660: You must explicitly define environment variables or map a volume into a
661: container in order to provide access to any other Secret.
662: 
663: There may be Secrets for several Pods on the same node. However, only the
664: Secrets that a Pod requests are potentially visible within its containers.
665: Therefore, one Pod does not have access to the Secrets of another Pod.
666: 
667: ### Configure least-privilege access to Secrets
668: 
669: To enhance the security measures around Secrets, use separate namespaces to isolate access to mounted secrets.
670: 
671: {{< warning >}}
672: Any containers that run with `privileged: true` on a node can access all
673: Secrets used on that node.
674: {{< /warning >}}
675: 
676: ## {{% heading "whatsnext" %}}
677: 
678: - For guidelines to manage and improve the security of your Secrets, refer to
679:   [Good practices for Kubernetes Secrets](/docs/concepts/security/secrets-good-practices).
680: - Learn how to [manage Secrets using `kubectl`](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-kubectl/)
681: - Learn how to [manage Secrets using config file](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-config-file/)
682: - Learn how to [manage Secrets using kustomize](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-kustomize/)
683: - Read the [API reference](/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/config-and-storage-resources/secret-v1/) for `Secret`

76: ### Spread constraint definition
77: 
78: You can define one or multiple `topologySpreadConstraints` entries to instruct the
79: kube-scheduler how to place each incoming Pod in relation to the existing Pods across
80: your cluster. Those fields are:
81: 
82: - **maxSkew** describes the degree to which Pods may be unevenly distributed. You must
83:   specify this field and the number must be greater than zero. Its semantics differ
84:   according to the value of `whenUnsatisfiable`:
85: 
86:   - if you select `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`, then `maxSkew` defines the
87:     maximum permitted difference between the number of matching pods in the target
88:     topology and the _global minimum_
89:     (the minimum number of matching pods in an eligible domain or zero if the number of eligible domains is less than MinDomains).
90:     For example, if you have 3 zones with 2, 2 and 1 matching pods respectively,
91:     `MaxSkew` is set to 1 then the global minimum is 1.
92:   - if you select `whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway`, the scheduler gives higher
93:     precedence to topologies that would help reduce the skew.
94: 
95: - **minDomains** indicates a minimum number of eligible domains. This field is optional.
96:   A domain is a particular instance of a topology. An eligible domain is a domain whose
97:   nodes match the node selector.
98: 
99:   <!-- OK to remove this note once v1.29 Kubernetes is out of support -->
100:   {{< note >}}
101:   Before Kubernetes v1.30, the `minDomains` field was only available if the
102:   `MinDomainsInPodTopologySpread` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates-removed/)
103:   was enabled (default since v1.28). In older Kubernetes clusters it might be explicitly
104:   disabled or the field might not be available.
105:   {{< /note >}}
106: 
107:   - The value of `minDomains` must be greater than 0, when specified.
108:     You can only specify `minDomains` in conjunction with `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`.
109:   - When the number of eligible domains with match topology keys is less than `minDomains`,
110:     Pod topology spread treats global minimum as 0, and then the calculation of `skew` is performed.
111:     The global minimum is the minimum number of matching Pods in an eligible domain,
112:     or zero if the number of eligible domains is less than `minDomains`.
113:   - When the number of eligible domains with matching topology keys equals or is greater than
114:     `minDomains`, this value has no effect on scheduling.
115:   - If you do not specify `minDomains`, the constraint behaves as if `minDomains` is 1.
116: 
117: - **topologyKey** is the key of [node labels](#node-labels). Nodes that have a label with this key
118: 	and identical values are considered to be in the same topology.
119:   We call each instance of a topology (in other words, a <key, value> pair) a domain. The scheduler
120:   will try to put a balanced number of pods into each domain.
121: 	Also, we define an eligible domain as a domain whose nodes meet the requirements of
122: 	nodeAffinityPolicy and nodeTaintsPolicy.
123: 
124: - **whenUnsatisfiable** indicates how to deal with a Pod if it doesn't satisfy the spread constraint:
125:   - `DoNotSchedule` (default) tells the scheduler not to schedule it.
126:   - `ScheduleAnyway` tells the scheduler to still schedule it while prioritizing nodes that minimize the skew.
127: 
128: - **labelSelector** is used to find matching Pods. Pods
129:   that match this label selector are counted to determine the
130:   number of Pods in their corresponding topology domain.
131:   See [Label Selectors](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#label-selectors)
132:   for more details.

135:   spreading will be calculated. The keys are used to lookup values from the pod labels,
136:   those key-value labels are ANDed with `labelSelector` to select the group of existing
137:   pods over which spreading will be calculated for the incoming pod. The same key is
138:   forbidden to exist in both `matchLabelKeys` and `labelSelector`. `matchLabelKeys` cannot
139:   be set when `labelSelector` isn't set. Keys that don't exist in the pod labels will be
140:   ignored. A null or empty list means only match against the `labelSelector`.
141: 
142:   With `matchLabelKeys`, you don't need to update the `pod.spec` between different revisions.
143:   The controller/operator just needs to set different values to the same label key for different
144:   revisions. The scheduler will assume the values automatically based on `matchLabelKeys`. For

146:   [pod-template-hash](/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#pod-template-hash-label), which
147:   is added automatically by the Deployment controller, to distinguish between different revisions
148:   in a single Deployment.
149: 
150:   ```yaml
151:       topologySpreadConstraints:
152:           - maxSkew: 1
153:             topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
154:             whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
155:             labelSelector:
156:               matchLabels:
157:                 app: foo
158:             matchLabelKeys:
159:               - pod-template-hash

162:   {{< note >}}
163:   The `matchLabelKeys` field is a beta-level field and enabled by default in 1.27. You can disable it by disabling the
164:   `MatchLabelKeysInPodTopologySpread` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/).
165:   {{< /note >}}
166: 
167: - **nodeAffinityPolicy** indicates how we will treat Pod's nodeAffinity/nodeSelector
168:   when calculating pod topology spread skew. Options are:
169:   - Honor: only nodes matching nodeAffinity/nodeSelector are included in the calculations.
170:   - Ignore: nodeAffinity/nodeSelector are ignored. All nodes are included in the calculations.
171: 
172:   If this value is null, the behavior is equivalent to the Honor policy.
173: 
174:   {{< note >}}
175:   The `nodeAffinityPolicy` is a beta-level field and enabled by default in 1.26. You can disable it by disabling the
176:   `NodeInclusionPolicyInPodTopologySpread` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/).
177:   {{< /note >}}
178: 
179: - **nodeTaintsPolicy** indicates how we will treat node taints when calculating
180:   pod topology spread skew. Options are:
181:   - Honor: nodes without taints, along with tainted nodes for which the incoming pod
182:     has a toleration, are included.
183:   - Ignore: node taints are ignored. All nodes are included.
184: 
185:   If this value is null, the behavior is equivalent to the Ignore policy.
186: 
187:   {{< note >}}
188:   The `nodeTaintsPolicy` is a beta-level field and enabled by default in 1.26. You can disable it by disabling the
189:   `NodeInclusionPolicyInPodTopologySpread` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/).
190:   {{< /note >}}
191: 
192: When a Pod defines more than one `topologySpreadConstraint`, those constraints are
193: combined using a logical AND operation: the kube-scheduler looks for a node for the incoming Pod
194: that satisfies all the configured constraints.
195: 
196: ### Node labels
197: 
198: Topology spread constraints rely on node labels to identify the topology
199: domain(s) that each {{< glossary_tooltip text="node" term_id="node" >}} is in.

75: 
76: Kubernetes implements horizontal pod autoscaling as a control loop that runs intermittently
77: (it is not a continuous process). The interval is set by the
78: `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period` parameter to the
79: [`kube-controller-manager`](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-controller-manager/)
80: (and the default interval is 15 seconds).
81: 
82: Once during each period, the controller manager queries the resource utilization against the
83: metrics specified in each HorizontalPodAutoscaler definition. The controller manager
84: finds the target resource defined by the `scaleTargetRef`,
85: then selects the pods based on the target resource's `.spec.selector` labels,
86: and obtains the metrics from either the resource metrics API (for per-pod resource metrics),
87: or the custom metrics API (for all other metrics).
88: 
89: - For per-pod resource metrics (like CPU), the controller fetches the metrics
90:   from the resource metrics API for each Pod targeted by the HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
91:   Then, if a target utilization value is set, the controller calculates the utilization
92:   value as a percentage of the equivalent
93:   [resource request](/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/#requests-and-limits)
94:   on the containers in each Pod. If a target raw value is set, the raw metric values are used directly.
95:   The controller then takes the mean of the utilization or the raw value (depending on the type
96:   of target specified) across all targeted Pods, and produces a ratio used to scale
97:   the number of desired replicas.
98: 
99:   Please note that if some of the Pod's containers do not have the relevant resource request set,
100:   CPU utilization for the Pod will not be defined and the autoscaler will
101:   not take any action for that metric. See the [algorithm details](#algorithm-details) section below
102:   for more information about how the autoscaling algorithm works.
103: 
104: - For per-pod custom metrics, the controller functions similarly to per-pod resource metrics,
105:   except that it works with raw values, not utilization values.
106: 
107: - For object metrics and external metrics, a single metric is fetched, which describes
108:   the object in question. This metric is compared to the target
109:   value, to produce a ratio as above. In the `autoscaling/v2` API
110:   version, this value can optionally be divided by the number of Pods before the
111:   comparison is made.
112: 
113: The common use for HorizontalPodAutoscaler is to configure it to fetch metrics from
114: {{< glossary_tooltip text="aggregated APIs" term_id="aggregation-layer" >}}
115: (`metrics.k8s.io`, `custom.metrics.k8s.io`, or `external.metrics.k8s.io`). The `metrics.k8s.io` API is
116: usually provided by an add-on named Metrics Server, which needs to be launched separately.
117: For more information about resource metrics, see
118: [Metrics Server](/docs/tasks/debug/debug-cluster/resource-metrics-pipeline/#metrics-server).
119: 
120: [Support for metrics APIs](#support-for-metrics-apis) explains the stability guarantees and support status for these
121: different APIs.
122: 
123: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller accesses corresponding workload resources that support scaling (such as Deployments
124: and StatefulSet). These resources each have a subresource named `scale`, an interface that allows you to dynamically set the
125: number of replicas and examine each of their current states.
126: For general information about subresources in the Kubernetes API, see
127: [Kubernetes API Concepts](/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/).
128: 
129: ### Algorithm details
130: 
131: From the most basic perspective, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
132: operates on the ratio between desired metric value and current metric
133: value:
134: 
135: ```math
136: \begin{equation*}
137: desiredReplicas = ceil\left\lceil currentReplicas \times \frac{currentMetricValue}{desiredMetricValue} \right\rceil
138: \end{equation*}
139: ```
140: 
141: For example, if the current metric value is `200m`, and the desired value
142: is `100m`, the number of replicas will be doubled, since
143: \\( { 200.0 \div 100.0 } = 2.0 \\).  
144: If the current value is instead `50m`, you'll halve the number of
145: replicas, since \\( { 50.0 \div 100.0 } = 0.5 \\). The control plane skips any scaling
146: action if the ratio is sufficiently close to 1.0 (within a globally-configurable
147: tolerance, 0.1 by default).
148: 
149: When a `targetAverageValue` or `targetAverageUtilization` is specified,
150: the `currentMetricValue` is computed by taking the average of the given
151: metric across all Pods in the HorizontalPodAutoscaler's scale target.
152: 
153: Before checking the tolerance and deciding on the final values, the control
154: plane also considers whether any metrics are missing, and how many Pods
155: are [`Ready`](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-conditions).
156: All Pods with a deletion timestamp set (objects with a deletion timestamp are
157: in the process of being shut down / removed) are ignored, and all failed Pods
158: are discarded.
159: 
160: If a particular Pod is missing metrics, it is set aside for later; Pods
161: with missing metrics will be used to adjust the final scaling amount.
162: 
163: When scaling on CPU, if any pod has yet to become ready (it's still
164: initializing, or possibly is unhealthy) _or_ the most recent metric point for
165: the pod was before it became ready, that pod is set aside as well.
166: 
167: Due to technical constraints, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
168: cannot exactly determine the first time a pod becomes ready when
169: determining whether to set aside certain CPU metrics. Instead, it
170: considers a Pod "not yet ready" if it's unready and transitioned to
171: ready within a short, configurable window of time since it started.
172: This value is configured with the `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-initial-readiness-delay`
173: flag, and its default is 30 seconds.
174: Once a pod has become ready, it considers any transition to
175: ready to be the first if it occurred within a longer, configurable time
176: since it started. This value is configured with the
177: `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-cpu-initialization-period` flag, and its
178: default is 5 minutes.
179: 
180: The \\( currentMetricValue \over desiredMetricValue \\) base scale ratio is then
181: calculated, using the remaining pods not set aside or discarded from above.
182: 
183: If there were any missing metrics, the control plane recomputes the average more
184: conservatively, assuming those pods were consuming 100% of the desired
185: value in case of a scale down, and 0% in case of a scale up. This dampens
186: the magnitude of any potential scale.
187: 
188: Furthermore, if any not-yet-ready pods were present, and the workload would have
189: scaled up without factoring in missing metrics or not-yet-ready pods,
190: the controller conservatively assumes that the not-yet-ready pods are consuming 0%
191: of the desired metric, further dampening the magnitude of a scale up.
192: 
193: After factoring in the not-yet-ready pods and missing metrics, the
194: controller recalculates the usage ratio. If the new ratio reverses the scale
195: direction, or is within the tolerance, the controller doesn't take any scaling
196: action. In other cases, the new ratio is used to decide any change to the
197: number of Pods.
198: 
199: Note that the _original_ value for the average utilization is reported
200: back via the HorizontalPodAutoscaler status, without factoring in the
201: not-yet-ready pods or missing metrics, even when the new usage ratio is
202: used.
203: 
204: If multiple metrics are specified in a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, this
205: calculation is done for each metric, and then the largest of the desired
206: replica counts is chosen. If any of these metrics cannot be converted
207: into a desired replica count (e.g. due to an error fetching the metrics
208: from the metrics APIs) and a scale down is suggested by the metrics which
209: can be fetched, scaling is skipped. This means that the HPA is still capable
210: of scaling up if one or more metrics give a `desiredReplicas` greater than
211: the current value.
212: 
213: Finally, right before HPA scales the target, the scale recommendation is recorded. The
214: controller considers all recommendations within a configurable window choosing the
215: highest recommendation from within that window. This value can be configured using the
216: `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-downscale-stabilization` flag, which defaults to 5 minutes.
217: This means that scaledowns will occur gradually, smoothing out the impact of rapidly
218: fluctuating metric values.
219:

561: Because Pods represent processes running on nodes in the cluster, it is important to
562: allow those processes to gracefully terminate when they are no longer needed (rather
563: than being abruptly stopped with a `KILL` signal and having no chance to clean up).
564: 
565: The design aim is for you to be able to request deletion and know when processes
566: terminate, but also be able to ensure that deletes eventually complete.
567: When you request deletion of a Pod, the cluster records and tracks the intended grace period
568: before the Pod is allowed to be forcefully killed. With that forceful shutdown tracking in
569: place, the {{< glossary_tooltip text="kubelet" term_id="kubelet" >}} attempts graceful
570: shutdown.
571: 
572: Typically, with this graceful termination of the pod, kubelet makes requests to the container runtime to attempt to stop the containers in the pod by first sending a TERM (aka. SIGTERM) signal, with a grace period timeout, to the main process in each container. The requests to stop the containers are processed by the container runtime asynchronously. There is no guarantee to the order of processing for these requests. Many container runtimes respect the `STOPSIGNAL` value defined in the container image and, if different, send the container image configured STOPSIGNAL instead of TERM.
573: Once the grace period has expired, the KILL signal is sent to any remaining
574: processes, and the Pod is then deleted from the
575: {{< glossary_tooltip text="API Server" term_id="kube-apiserver" >}}. If the kubelet or the
576: container runtime's management service is restarted while waiting for processes to terminate, the
577: cluster retries from the start including the full original grace period.
578: 
579: Pod termination flow, illustrated with an example:
580: 
581: 1. You use the `kubectl` tool to manually delete a specific Pod, with the default grace period
582:    (30 seconds).
583: 
584: 1. The Pod in the API server is updated with the time beyond which the Pod is considered "dead"
585:    along with the grace period.
586:    If you use `kubectl describe` to check the Pod you're deleting, that Pod shows up as "Terminating".
587:    On the node where the Pod is running: as soon as the kubelet sees that a Pod has been marked
588:    as terminating (a graceful shutdown duration has been set), the kubelet begins the local Pod
589:    shutdown process.
590: 
591:    1. If one of the Pod's containers has defined a `preStop`
592:       [hook](/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks) and the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`
593:       in the Pod spec is not set to 0, the kubelet runs that hook inside of the container.
594:       The default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting is 30 seconds.
595: 
596:       If the `preStop` hook is still running after the grace period expires, the kubelet requests
597:       a small, one-off grace period extension of 2 seconds.
598:    {{% note %}}
599:    If the `preStop` hook needs longer to complete than the default grace period allows,
600:    you must modify `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to suit this.
601:    {{% /note %}}
602: 
603:    1. The kubelet triggers the container runtime to send a TERM signal to process 1 inside each
604:       container.
605: 
606:       There is [special ordering](#termination-with-sidecars) if the Pod has any
607:       {{< glossary_tooltip text="sidecar containers" term_id="sidecar-container" >}} defined.
608:       Otherwise, the containers in the Pod receive the TERM signal at different times and in
609:       an arbitrary order. If the order of shutdowns matters, consider using a `preStop` hook
610:       to synchronize (or switch to using sidecar containers).

612: 1. At the same time as the kubelet is starting graceful shutdown of the Pod, the control plane
613:    evaluates whether to remove that shutting-down Pod from EndpointSlice (and Endpoints) objects,
614:    where those objects represent a {{< glossary_tooltip term_id="service" text="Service" >}}

619:    Pods that shut down slowly should not continue to serve regular traffic and should start
